messages.subject: Statistical model for Likert scales
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a question concerning the choice of an appropriate model for
testing Likert scale results from a questionnaire on language
attitudes and use in Namibia.
A colleague recommended using the "lrm" model included in the rms-
library (following Baayen 2008, 208-14). In some points, however, the
results turn out very counter-intuitive.
For a question "Do you use language x talking to your family" (from
1=never to 5=always) the model found AGE to be significant for the use
of English, ETHNICITY for German and Afrikaans (which reflects the
answers), but no significance whatsoever for an indigenous language,
although the native African participants mostly had 4 or 5 and the
white participants mostly had 1.
Is there a flaw in the choice of the model? Are the token numbers (67
participants) too low? Other problems?

Below are the results of the first run (in a second we excluded the
non-significant vectors, but the result stayed the same) for Afrikaans
(AFR) and indigenous language (IDG). (Sorry about the odd format, is
there a way to make this look better in a post?).

My colleague suspects that in the
Frequencies of Responses (for IDG)
 1  2  3  4  5
34  1  1 10 19
the low figures for "2" and "3" might pose a problem.

The data file looks as follows:
NUMBER	ETHNICITY	YEAR_BIRTH	GENDER	AFR	ENG	GER	IDG
1	boer	1989	f	5	2	1	1
2	boer	1986	m	4	2	1	1
3	boer	1984	f	5	2	1	1
4	boer	1983	m	5	2	1	1
(...)

And my second question would be: Is there a model we can use to test
all four languages in one rush? Or is it recommendable to do every
language separately?

Many thanks in advance and best wishes,
Alex

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alexander,

having empty or very low-frequency categories can be a problem for the model. A possible solution is to collapse the 5 categories in only two (0,1) and run a logistic regression having the newly binary variable as your response. As a matter of fact the responses you showed us do seem to have a "natural" binary structure (the extremes 1 and 5 are highly populated).

If you do this you can use the glm() function and specify the "logit" link for the binomial family of generalized linear models.

cheers & luck!

pep vallbé

Political Science Department
University of Barcelona

messages.body_plain:
Yes, the low frequencies will be quite problematic so conflation with
other levels might help. The more important thing to me at least
however is that I really think that, whatever model you end up
fitting, it should be run on a data frame containing data for all the
languages (LANG, with the levels AFR, IDG, ...) in another column and
then use the model formula.

RESPONSE ~ (GENDER + AGE + ETHNICITY + LANG)^2

STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
-----------------------------------------------
University of California, Santa Barbara
http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries
-----------------------------------------------

(A+B+C)^2
   =

STG

messages.subject: Interpretation of lrm output
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have some questions concerning the interpretation of lrm output (hopefully not too trivial).

As posted elsewhere I'm doing a study on language use in Namibia on the basis of a questionnaire with 5-point likert scales.
I want to test if the usage in particular situations of one of the 4 languages spoken there is influenced by the following factors:
 $ ETHNICITY : 4 levels "boer","ger","misc", "nat_afr"
 $ GENDER    : 2 levels "f","m"
 $ AGE

E.g., for the usage of English (ENG) in a certain situation, I first identify significant factors using,
QUEST.LRM = lrm(ENG ~ GENDER+AGE+ETHNICITY, data=QUEST, x=T, y=T)
anova(QUEST.LRM)

then I simplify the model (eliminate GENDER; not significant):
QUEST.LRMA = lrm(ENG ~ AGE+ETHNICITY, data=QUEST, x=T, y=T)

then
anova(QUEST.LRMA)
yields:

Factor     Chi-Square d.f. P

 AGE        12.23      1    0.0005

 ETHNICITY  12.15      3    0.0069

 TOTAL      16.82      4    0.0021
QUEST.LRMA
looks as follows:

                  Coef    S.E.   Wald Z Pr(>|Z|)
y>=2               2.2462 0.9452  2.38  0.0175
y>=3               1.1175 0.9241  1.21  0.2266
y>=4               0.6153 0.9239  0.67  0.5054
y>=5              -0.5646 0.9327 -0.61  0.5450

ETHNICITY=ger      3.3409 1.0494  3.18  0.0015
ETHNICITY=misc     3.1383 1.1810  2.66  0.0079
ETHNICITY=nat_afr  1.1425 0.6576  1.74  0.0823

And here are my questions concerning what exactly is significant about ETHNICITY and AGE:

- can I interpret the results as follows: ETHNICITY=ger and ETHNICITY=misc are significant (p<.05); the fact that they have a positive coef means that the respective variable (ENG) is favoured, (if negative --> disfavoured)

- why are only three of my four ETHNICITY levels (ger, misc, nat_afr) displayed?

- for the interpretation of how age is significant, I need the summary(QUEST.LRMA), don't I?

messages.body_plain:
You would include interactions as usual, i.e. either as A:B or A*B. As
for the interpretation of the model, I would do that via the predicted
probabilities. Generate all combinations of variable levels/values in
your predictor space with expand.grid, compute predicted probabilities
of the levels of the dependent variable, and plot them for the
significant predictors. That usually makes even more complex results
fairly comprehensible.

Cheers,

STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries
